title: Fort Tejon, Randsburg tours offer hands-on search for the paranormal

content:
Scary movies and haunts are fun but maybe you’re seeking some real-life thrills. Paranormal investigator Marie Mason has some hands-on supernatural adventures set this month that are both just a short drive away.

First up, she and her team will return to Fort Tejon State Historic Park, which she last investigated in April.

Mason is excited to be back at the former U.S. Army base in October, a month that previously had been booked for other events.

"Fort Tejon is very, very spooky," she said, recalling her experience during an initial walkthrough five years ago. "My spider senses go way up."

Steered away from certain locations on site, Mason said she ventured to the forest on the grounds.

"It's a forest of oak trees, and oak trees are very, very ancient. We're talking 500-year-old oak trees, very old. OK, it's magical. it's magical for real. So I start wandering over there. I feel something over here, like it's spooky, and I walk and then I see this, lo and behold, I see this well, an old well with some sticks in it and some water, and I'm like, 'Bingo, something was over here.'"

This tour will include an exploration of the officer's house, a two-story preserved colonial-style residence that the tour will investigate beyond the plexi glass, and the haunted oak tree, where early settler Peter Lebeck was buried after a fatal run-in with a bear in 1837.

Other locations on the tour will be the barracks, with Army uniforms, hats, beds,and hospital artifacts that have activated equipment on previous outings; the quartermaster/carpenter's tool area, featuring artifacts in their original positions (some behind protective barriers; and the blacksmith building, which has been an active site during previous visits.

Steven Ptomey, the district chief of cultural resources for the Great Basin District of California State Parks, said even the real-life artifacts can be terrifying.

He said, "There was a hospital there at the fort at one time. And if you go through the barracks, you see a display, there's a small model of the hospital and there's also a surgeon’s Army amputation kit. That kit can give you nightmares because it's like Freddy Krueger, right?

"It's just all knives and saws and all that kind of stuff. I was an army medic myself back in the ‘80s, and I look at that and it's like, ‘Oh my gosh,’ because I have dealt with a few serious injuries when I was in (the service), and that kit kind of scares me. The thought of having to do that (surgery) with no anesthetic other than probably whiskey. Well, whiskey or opium."

Ptomey, who stays on site at the park during the week, has noticed some unexplained phenomena while driving past the fort's cemetery.

"My state car is a Tesla, and it has a display of people and things that are on the road. Sometimes, when I drive past the cemetery, it'll show a figure like a person is standing there, and, of course, there's nobody standing there.

"So the first time that happened, that was a little creepy. I was coming back from another assignment in another part of the state ... and that kind of creeped me out. Now it happens occasionally. I'd like to think it's a glitch in the software, but I don't know."

Mason said part of the fun is being out in the open to explore the buildings and surrounding areas.

"The main thing about Fort Tejon is, it's different. You're not going into the Queen Mary in a controlled environment. You're not going in a hotel room. It's a full park that's still run by the state and as military guys, you know, and that's spooky."

For the tours, Mason will offer equipment to use including Kinect SLS (structured light sensor) and night vision cameras; SB7 Spirit Boxes; DNA Alice Boxes, a tool of instrumental trans-communication technology; Estes Method headset; and REM Pods, which uses an electromagnetic field (EMF) to search for disturbances.

Attendees are also welcome to bring their own equipment.

After visiting Fort Tejon, Mason will lead two days of investigations in her new hometown of Randburg on Oct. 30 and 31.

The Mojave Desert gold rush town sprang up nearly overnight in 1895 following a more than $60 million gold discovery. Hopeful prospectors set up saloons, churches, schools, gambling parlors, brothels and even an opera house.

Once the gold was mined, the town endured, with many original buildings still intact and a stubborn and dedicated community keeping it a draw for tourists.

Mason said, "Randsburg is haunted, beyond belief, and the majority of the town doesn't like to admit it. I found out by living here that the reason is that they're scared, because they see them (ghosts). These old-timers, they start yelling at me about 'you and your ghosting,' and I'd be, like, 'Wow, you know, I'm just trying to keep history alive, dude.' Then I realized over time, it was because they're scared."

The tours here will include stops at the Haunted Underground Speakeasy; the 1895 Ice House, where something has been seen in the attic; the Old Corner Bar; the Miner’s Poker Murder Cabin, which was the site of a deadly 1917 poker game shootout; the old jail, where visitors can bring a quarter to “bail out” the ladies of the night; the Chime Shop, with a haunted mirror where guests can take a selfie.

A trolley will take attendees to the different locations during the tour, which will run at least 90 minutes.

VIP ticket holders will also enjoy a three-course dinner with tri-tip, salad, sides and a drink plus a bar token for The Joint Saloon ($5 value).

Attendees can even make it a full haunted weekend with cabins, short-term rentals, hotel rooms and RV spots available to stay overnight in the real ghost town.

Randsburg tours will be held at 7, 8:30 and 10 p.m. Oct. 30; and 6, 7, 8:30, 9 and 10 p.m. Oct. 31 starting at 180 Butte Ave. in Randsburg.

Admission for the Oct. 30 tours is $55.20 (includes fee) for 7 p.m., $60.54 for 8:30 or 10 p.m. The Oct. 31 tour admission is $60.54 for 6 p.m., $65.87 for 7 p.m., $71.21 for 8:30 p.m., $76.54 for 9 or 10 p.m. 

VIP tickets, which include dinner and the tour, are $92.55 for all times Oct. 30 and 31 except the 9 p.m. Oct. 30 tour, which is $100.01.

Attendees under age 12 pay $17.85 for the tour.

Fort Tejon guests can take part in one of three investigations at 7, 8:30 or 10 p.m. Oct. 24 at the park, 4201 Fort Tejon Road in Lebec.

Admission is $71.21 (includes fee) for 7 p.m., $86.14 for 8:30 p.m. and $92.55 for 10 p.m. Children under age 12 (who must be accompanied by a guardian) pay $28.52 for any tour.

Note that some ticket sales end this week so visit Eventbrite.com ASAP to reserve your spot.
